| [NOTE-763](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-763.md) v2 | Calo et al. — Distances for Markov chains from sample streams | The bicausal transport distance between two finite Markov chains, which the authors' earlier paper identified with the bisimulation metric, has a second linear program whose constraints use only the chains' discounted state-transition occupancy measures, not their kernels. A stochastic primal-dual method on it gets an ε-accurate estimate with probability 1−δ from O((\|X\|\|Y\|(\|X\|+\|Y\|) + (\|X\|+\|Y\|) log(1/δ)) / ((1−γ)²ε²)) independent transition samples per chain. The guarantee assumes independent draws from the occupancy measures, which needs restarts; samples from one running trajectory are outside it. | Read |
| [NOTE-784](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-784.md) v2 | Coifman et al. — Diffusion maps | From a symmetric, positivity-preserving, positive semi-definite kernel, normalized into a Markov operator conjugate to a symmetric one, the top eigenfunctions scaled by powers of their eigenvalues embed the data so that Euclidean distance equals diffusion distance. A one-parameter normalization separates geometry from sampling density, recovering the Laplace–Beltrami operator at α = 1. The symmetry of the kernel is what yields the spectral decomposition; non-symmetric kernels are not treated. | Superseded — by [NOTE-1441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1441.md) |
| [NOTE-787](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-787.md) v2 | Vereshchagin & Vitányi — Kolmogorov's structure functions and model selection | For a string x of length n and every complexity bound α, the minimal two-part code length λ_x(α), the structure function h_x(α) + α and the best achievable fit β_x(α) + K(x) are one function to within O(log n), and any set witnessing λ_x or h_x also witnesses β_x. Every non-increasing shape occurs for some x. h_x and λ_x are upper semicomputable but not computable; β_x is not even semicomputable. Finite sets only; the extension to computable distributions costs O(log n). | Read |
| [NOTE-790](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-790.md) | Vitányi — Meaningful Information | With total recursive functions as models, the shortest model that completes an optimal two-part code for a string (its sophistication) is a non-trivial split of its information into structure and noise. With partial recursive models the split collapses to zero for every string. The total-function, computable-distribution and finite-set classes agree to within logarithmic terms. Some strings of every length are almost all structure, and sophistication is not computable. | Read |
| [NOTE-814](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-814.md) | Salter-Duke — Tangled webs | An exact but exponential algorithm finds edge-connectivity tangles in graphs of up to about 200 vertices. On eleven small real networks, tangle communities resemble those of standard methods only where community structure is strongly delineated; three networks have no distinguishable tangles at the orders reached, and where tangles do distinguish regions, some hold only one to three vertices. On images, lines one pixel wide cannot be distinguished. The author concludes the tangle notion of cohesion "is not as compelling as I had hoped". | Read |
| [NOTE-817](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-817.md) | Sayed Ahmed — Back and forth between algebraic geometry, algebraic logic, sheaves and forcing | Distributive lattices with join-preserving idempotent operators are represented, after Comer, as continuous sections of a sheaf of quotient algebras over the prime spectrum of their fixed-point part. A small site is said to give a notion of forcing, with Kripke–Joyal clauses, and a Łukasiewicz conjunction is forced through a tensor product. Most theorems are stated without proof, and negation is never written out. | Read |
| [NOTE-821](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-821.md) | Kupiainen — Rigorous renormalization group | A three-page orientation by a principal of rigorous RG. It covers Wilson's block-spin map as an iteration on Hamiltonians, made rigorous by cluster (polymer) expansions that control large fields, and what this proved. The massless 4D lattice φ⁴ model is Gaussian at long distances. The continuum 4D φ⁴ limit is always Gaussian (Aizenman and Duminil-Copin). The Gross–Neveu model and Hall-conductivity universality have been constructed or proved. The method stays near Gaussian, and a non-perturbative formalism is missing. The piece makes no new claim of its own. | Read |
| [NOTE-822](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-822.md) | Ovsjanikov et al. — Functional maps | A bijection T: M → N is fully encoded by the linear map f ↦ f∘T⁻¹ it induces on functions, a matrix C in chosen bases. If T preserves volume (or the bases are discretely orthonormal), C is orthogonal, so its inverse is its transpose; if T is an isometry, it commutes with the Laplace–Beltrami operator, so C maps each eigenspace to the matching one. Descriptor, landmark, segment and commutativity constraints are linear in C, so matching reduces to a least-squares solve with a 100-eigenfunction basis, which beat Blended Intrinsic Maps on SCAPE and TOSCA. | Read |
| [NOTE-824](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-824.md) | Pfau et al. — Spectral Inference Networks | For a symmetric kernel k on a space with a sampling density p, the span of the top N eigenfunctions of K[f](../../../record/notes.d/x) = E_x′[k(x,x′)f(x′)] maximizes Tr(Σ⁻¹Π) over functions, with Σ = E[uuᵀ] and Π = E[k(x,x′)u(x)u(x′)ᵀ]; a Cholesky-masked gradient orders them and moving averages of Σ and its Jacobian remove the minibatch bias. Slow Feature Analysis is the graph-Laplacian case. The ordering argument is informal by the authors' own statement, and the paper never considers contrastive kernels or positive pairs. | Read |
| [NOTE-829](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-829.md) | Jorgensen & Tian — Noncommutative Analysis (GNS, RKHS) | The book calls the kernel-to-Hilbert-space construction "the GNS construction" (Remark 1.34) and states that minimal realizations ϕ(x,y) = ⟨Φ(x), Φ(y)⟩ are unique up to a unitary (Cor. 1.35). It does not prove the corollary; the proof is "left as an exercise". The parallel uniqueness for states and cyclic representations is proved (Thm 4.35), and the argument transfers. The commutative GNS space L²(μ) is written out explicitly (Ex. 4.86, Lemma 3.28). | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-831](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-831.md) | Farrell & Ioannou — Generalized Stability Theory I | For a linear system du/dt = Au with A non-normal, the eigenvalues fix only the t → ∞ behaviour. Growth over a finite time t is the largest singular value of e^{At}, bounded below by the fastest mode and at t → 0 set by the numerical abscissa, the top eigenvalue of (A + A†)/2. A system with every mode damped can amplify a perturbation a hundredfold, and its forced and stochastic responses exceed those of the normal system with the same spectrum. | Read |
| [NOTE-836](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-836.md) | Schölkopf, Herbrich & Smola — A Generalized Representer Theorem | For any nonempty set X, real positive-definite kernel k, strictly increasing g and any cost c on the training triples, even coupled, non-convex or infinite-valued, every minimizer of c + g(‖f‖) over the class F of countable kernel expansions with finite RKHS norm is a finite expansion Σ α_i k(·, x_i) at the training points. The proof uses only the reproducing property and Pythagoras. Existence of a minimizer, the extension from F to the completed RKHS, and the semiparametric Theorem 2 are not proved here. | Read |
| [NOTE-837](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-837.md) | Bach — Information Theory with Kernel Methods | With a continuous kernel normalised to k(x,x) = 1 on a compact set, the uncentred covariance operator Σ_p is a density operator. Its quantum relative entropy is sandwiched between the KL of two kernel-smoothed distributions and the KL itself, D(p̃‖q̃) ≤ D(Σ_p‖Σ_q) ≤ D(p‖q), with equality on the right only for an orthonormal, hence discrete, embedding. On the torus the gap is O(σ²) in the bandwidth. Kernel mutual information characterizes independence; conditional independence only one way. | Read |
| [NOTE-838](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-838.md) | Muandet et al. — Kernel Mean Embedding of Distributions | A survey whose load-bearing chain is short and explicit. An RKHS is a Hilbert space with bounded evaluation, so Riesz gives k_x (Thm 2.4, Prop. 2.1). If E_P√k(X,X) < ∞, the expectation functional is bounded and Riesz gives μ_P with E_P f = ⟨f, μ_P⟩ (Lemma 3.1, proved). MMD is ‖μ_P − μ_Q‖ (eq. 3.29), a metric on distributions exactly when k is characteristic. HSIC is the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the centred cross-covariance. Every result is for a fixed kernel. | Read |
| [NOTE-839](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-839.md) | Trefethen et al. — Hydrodynamic Stability Without Eigenvalues | The linearized operators of plane Couette and Poiseuille flow are far from normal. With every eigenmode decaying, perturbations can grow transiently by O(R) and resonate by O(R²), and an operator perturbation of norm O(R⁻²) makes the flow eigenvalue-unstable, all read off the pseudospectra. That transition to turbulence then follows from linear growth plus energy-neutral nonlinear mixing is a conjecture, from a 2 × 2 model. | Read |
| [NOTE-842](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-842.md) | Farrell & Ioannou — Generalized Stability Theory II | For du/dt = A(t)u there are no modes, but the propagator's singular vectors and the Lyapunov exponents and vectors carry generalized stability theory over. A time-dependent operator that is stable, or neutral, at every instant can be asymptotically unstable, and only if it is non-normal. Random variation of the operator destabilizes generically, with less variation needed the more non-normal and the less damped the mean operator. | Read |
| [NOTE-843](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-843.md) | Gebhart, Hansen and Schrater — Knowledge Sheaves | A knowledge-graph embedding is a knowledge sheaf on the schema (one pair of restriction maps per relation type) with a 0-cochain of its pullback to the graph. The summed Structured Embedding score is the sheaf Laplacian form xᵀLx; adding a relation vector gives TransR, and identity maps TransE. Since the zero cochain is always a section, training needs negative triples and a margin. A multi-hop query is scored by harmonic extension, a Schur complement of the query graph's Laplacian, which beats summing TransE vectors on ip and pi queries. | Read |
| [NOTE-854](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-854.md) | Adler — Hilbert spaces and the Riesz representation theorem | An undergraduate expository proof, twice over, that every continuous linear functional on a Hilbert space is v ↦ ⟨u, v⟩ for a unique u with ‖u‖ = ‖φ‖: once from the projection theorem, once as u = Σ_k conj φ(e_k) e_k over any orthonormal basis, with ‖φ‖² = Σ_k \|φ(e_k)\|². It ends with von Neumann's proof of the Radon–Nikodym theorem for finite positive measures by applying Riesz to f ↦ ∫ f dν on L²(ν + μ). | Read |
| [NOTE-855](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-855.md) | Bra–ket notation (Wikipedia) | Dirac's notation writes vectors as kets and linear functionals as bras. On a Hilbert space the inner product, antilinear in its first slot, turns each ket into a bra, and the article cites the Riesz theorem for the reverse direction; on a Banach or untopologized space the bracket is only a functional applied to a vector, because Riesz does not apply. The article is a reference with internal inconsistencies, including an unsourced edit of 2026-09-30 to the date of the notation's origin. | Read |
| [NOTE-857](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-857.md) | Gelfand–Naimark–Segal construction (Wikipedia) | For a state ρ on a C*-algebra A, the semi-inner product ⟨a, b⟩ = ρ(b*a) on A, quotiented by its null left ideal and completed, carries A acting by left multiplication, with the class of the identity as a unit cyclic vector and ρ(a) = ⟨π(a)ξ, ξ⟩. Any two cyclic representations with cyclic vectors reproducing the same state are unitarily equivalent, by the unitary π(a)ξ ↦ π′(a)ξ′. The representation is irreducible exactly when the state is pure. The article says nothing about kernels. | Read |
| [NOTE-861](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-861.md) | Riesz representation theorem (Wikipedia) | On a real or complex Hilbert space every continuous linear functional φ is x ↦ ⟨x, f_φ⟩ for a unique f_φ, with ‖f_φ‖ = ‖φ‖; the map y ↦ ⟨·, y⟩ is an antilinear isometric bijection H → H*. Completeness is used only to split H = ker φ ⊕ (ker φ)^⊥. The article then defines the adjoint of a bounded operator between Hilbert spaces through this bijection, and shows it is the transpose read through the two Riesz maps. | Read |
| [NOTE-863](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-863.md) | Goldreich — Foundations of Cryptography, Vol. 1 (1995 fragments): computational indistinguishability and pseudorandom generators | In the 1995 draft of Volume 1, computational indistinguishability is a strictly coarser equivalence than statistical closeness, and the book proves this two ways. Proposition 3.3 does it unconditionally: a counting argument shows there are ensembles supported on at most 2^(n/2) strings that no circuit of size 2^(n/8) tells from uniform with gap 2^(−n/8) or more, but such an ensemble cannot be sampled efficiently. §3.3.1 shows that the output of any pseudorandom generator is statistically far from uniform yet, by definition, indistinguishable from it. That witness is efficiently samplable, and it needs pseudorandom generators, which exist if and only if one-way functions do (Theorem 3.29, stated without proof). That efficient post-processing preserves indistinguishability is set as Exercise 1 of §3.8.4, not proved in the text. All of this is asymptotic, about ensembles indexed by n, not about single pairs of distributions. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-880](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-880.md) | Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin & Luby — A pseudorandom generator from any one-way function | There is a pseudorandom generator if and only if there is a one-way function (Theorem 6.2.2), in the uniform setting: adversaries are algorithms, and every reduction is an oracle Turing machine that turns an adversary for the constructed generator into an inverter for the given function. The route runs one-way function → false entropy generator → pseudoentropy generator → pseudorandom generator, where "computational entropy" is the Shannon entropy of some P-samplable distribution that no adversary of the given strength tells apart from the output. The general reduction is only weak-preserving: composed literally it needs seeds of length n^34, and the paper's direct construction n^10. The paper attributes to Goldreich [G : 89] the equivalence of pseudorandom generators with P-samplable pairs that are computationally indistinguishable but statistically very different; with Theorem 6.2.2 that gives the one-way function form, but the paper never writes that combined sentence. | Read |
| [NOTE-891](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-891.md) | Yao — Should tables be sorted? | For storing a set of n keys from a universe {1,…,m} in a table so that the membership query (is x in S?) is answered with the fewest worst-case adaptive probes, Yao proves that when the table cells may hold only keys of S or a bounded number of pointer symbols, sorted order with binary search (⌈lg(n+1)⌉ probes) is optimal once m exceeds a Ramsey-number threshold N(n, p, q), whatever the arrangement rule, table size or hashing scheme. The threshold is astronomically large, and for small universes sorted order is beaten (one probe suffices for m = 3 with n = 2, and for m ≤ 2n − 2 with n > 2). The optimality also fails as soon as one cell may hold an arbitrary value from the universe: with a single extra "directory" cell, two probes suffice for m ≥ 2^{16n²}. Only query cost is counted; building the table is free and unconstrained, so the paper says nothing about the cost of arranging or about trading arrangement cost against lookups. | Read |
| [NOTE-893](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-893.md) | Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph & Sleator — Competitive snoopy caching | For a shared-bus multiprocessor whose caches can either keep a replicated block (and pay one bus cycle for every write to it) or drop it (and pay p to fetch it again if it is read), the paper gives counter-based on-line algorithms whose total bus cost on every request sequence is at most twice that of the best off-line algorithm, and proves that no deterministic on-line algorithm can guarantee better than 2. The rule is: drop a copy once the writes it has caused since it was last read have cost as much as refetching it. With a third option (reading or writing through without fetching) the lower bound rises to 3, and the algorithm given is 3-competitive ignoring writebacks, 4 counting them; with associative caches the bound becomes the paging ratio. The paper never names rent-or-buy or ski rental; its rent is upkeep paid on an idle copy, and its purchase is the refetch after dropping, the reverse orientation of building a bin. Costs are fixed constants, the guarantees are worst case only, and the authors call the practical significance "unclear". | Read |
| [NOTE-902](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-902.md) | Piatetsky-Shapiro — The optimal selection of secondary indices is NP-complete | For one relation, a known mix of equality queries and updates, single-attribute secondary indexes, and a fixed upkeep charge per index on each update, choosing the index set that minimizes average transaction cost is NP-hard: minimum set cover reduces to it, each subset becoming an attribute and each element a query that any one of its attributes' indexes can answer. The paper calls the problem NP-complete but states only the optimization version, and the proof is a sketch of about half a page. Storage is not in the model; the only price of an index is upkeep on updates. A variant with off-line updates under an update-cost budget is asserted NP-complete without proof. The paper does not cite or discuss Comer 1978. | Read |
| [NOTE-903](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-903.md) | Sleator & Tarjan — Amortized efficiency of list update and paging rules | For a list searched sequentially from the front, where reaching the i-th item costs i, moving each accessed item to the front costs at most twice what any other rule costs on the same sequence, including rules that know the whole sequence in advance (four times, counting move-to-front's own moves), with no probabilistic assumption. A fixed list sorted by access frequency, and the transpose and frequency-count rules, are not within any constant factor of that. Rearranging ahead of need never pays in this model (Theorem 3). For paging, where only a small fast memory is cheap, no rule that cannot see the future can do better in the worst case than n/(n − n_MIN + 1) times the offline optimum MIN, and LRU and FIFO attain that bound up to an additive n_MIN; with equal memories the ratio is the memory size. The model is a single linear list (or a two-level memory) with uniform items and access cost depending only on position; it says nothing about partitions, bins or search that is not a scan. | Read |
| [NOTE-905](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-905.md) | Indyk & Motwani — Approximate nearest neighbors: towards removing the curse of dimensionality | Approximate nearest-neighbour search in d dimensions reduces, with small overhead, to a decision problem (is there a point within r, or none within (1+ε)r), and that decision problem is solved by locality-sensitive hashing: if hash functions make near pairs collide with probability at least p1 and far pairs with at most p2, then n^ρ random hash tables with ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2) answer queries with O(n^ρ) hash evaluations in O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space, with constant success probability. For Hamming space by bit sampling, and for ℓ_p with p in [1, 2] by embedding, ρ ≤ 1/(1+ε) in the 1999 text (1/ε, for ε > 1, in STOC). The paper also gives the other end of the trade: Õ(d) query time for n·O(1/ε)^d or (nd)^{O(1)} preprocessing. It is an upper bound only: it proves no lower bound, does not claim its exponents are best, solves only the approximate problem with constant probability, and counts preprocessing as space. | Read |
| [NOTE-913](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-913.md) | Green, Karvounarakis & Tannen — Provenance semirings | Annotating each input tuple with an element of a commutative semiring, and computing union and projection with + and join with ·, gives one positive relational algebra (RA+) that is set semantics over the Booleans, bag semantics over the naturals, c-tables over positive Boolean expressions, event tables over sets of outcomes, and lineage over sets of tuple ids. The polynomials N[X] in the tuple ids are the most general such annotation: for any RA+ query and any commutative semiring K, the K-annotated answer is the provenance polynomial evaluated at the input's K-annotations (Theorem 4.3). For datalog the paper needs ω-continuous semirings and formal power series N∞⟦X⟧, with the analogous factorization (Theorem 6.4) and a criterion for infinite coefficients (Theorem 6.5). Everything is positive: no negation, difference or aggregation, and revaluing inputs can only remove output tuples, never add them; trust and deletion propagation are not treated. | Read |
| [NOTE-914](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-914.md) | Panigrahy, Talwar & Wieder — Lower bounds on near neighbor search via metric expansion | Cell-probe lower bounds for near-neighbour search follow from the expansion of the graph joining points within distance r: a deterministic t-probe structure with m cells of w bits must have (mwt/n)^t at least the vertex expansion, and a randomized one must have m^t w/n at least the robust expansion at measure 1/m^t, on random data sets with weakly overlapping neighbourhoods. For the hypercube this recovers known bounds and gives, for example, space n^{1+Ω(1/(ct))} for approximation c and n^{Ω(1/(tε²))} for 1 + ε; for symmetric (Cayley) graphs a one-probe structure matches the bound, and for dynamic low-contention structures the update time must be at least the robust expansion over poly(t). The bounds are average case, for approximate decision search, and weak in t: they fall off exponentially in the number of probes, so they are tight only for a constant number of probes and say little about structures that probe n^ρ cells. | Read |
| [NOTE-917](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-917.md) | Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan & Shaft — When is "nearest neighbor" meaningful? | For a fixed number n of data points and a query drawn independently of them, if the variance of the p-th power of the query-to-point distance, divided by its mean, goes to zero as dimension m grows, then the farthest point is, with probability tending to one, within any factor 1 + ε of the nearest (Theorem 1). The condition holds for IID dimensions and for several correlated or non-identical workloads, and fails when data and queries lie on a low-dimensional subspace or when queries fall inside well-separated clusters. Simulations put the collapse of contrast within 10 to 20 dimensions for IID data, and two real image-feature sets showed weak contrast. The condition is sufficient, not shown necessary; the theorem is about the ratio of distances with n held fixed, and says nothing about real data of low intrinsic dimension except that such data can escape it. | Read |
| [NOTE-918](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-918.md) | Andoni, Laarhoven, Razenshteyn & Waingarten — Optimal hashing-based time–space trade-offs for approximate near neighbors | For c-approximate near-neighbour search (find a point within cr when one lies within r) over n points in Euclidean space, the paper gives a data structure for every pair of exponents with c²√ρq + (c²−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c²−1), using space n^{1+ρu+o(1)} + O(dn) and query time n^{ρq+o(1)} + dn^{o(1)}, on worst-case data (for Hamming and ℓ_1, c√ρq + (c−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c−1)). It proves the curve cannot be beaten by list-of-points structures, the model of all known data-independent hashing schemes, on random instances, and unconditionally in the cell-probe model only at one end (query n^{o(1)}) for one or two probes. So the exact trade between space spent organizing and per-query time is known within the hashing model; outside that model, for more than two probes, it is not, and data-dependent schemes are covered only by conjecture. | Read |
| [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md) | Kleinberg — The small-world phenomenon: an algorithmic perspective | On an n × n lattice where each node also gets q long-range links drawn with probability proportional to d^(−r), short paths exist for r = 0, but no algorithm that sees only the links of nodes the message has visited finds them faster than about n^(2/3) steps in expectation. At r = 2 the greedy rule (pass to the contact nearest the target in lattice distance) delivers in O((log n)²) expected steps (proved for p = q = 1); for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such algorithm needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))). So efficient decentralized search depends on how the long-range links are distributed relative to the lattice, not on the links' existence or on the graph's diameter. The k-dimensional version (r = k) is stated without proof, and the model is a lattice with a known distance that every node can compute to the target. | Read |
| [NOTE-925](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-925.md) | Larsen & Nelson — optimality of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma | For n, d ≥ 2 and lg^0.5001 n / √min{n, d} < ε < 1 there is an n-point set in R^d such that every map into R^m, linear or not, that keeps all squared distances within 1 ± ε needs m = Ω(ε⁻² lg(ε²n)), which is Ω(ε⁻² lg n) once ε > 1/min{n, d}^0.4999. So the Johnson–Lindenstrauss bound is optimal up to a constant, and the distributional lemma plus a union bound is the best route. The proof is an encoding argument over k-sparse point sets with k = ε⁻²/256, and the count it ends on is m = Ω(k lg(d/k)). | Read |
| [NOTE-926](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-926.md) | Achlioptas — database-friendly random projections | A random projection keeps all pairwise distances of n points within 1 ± ε with probability at least 1 − n^−β when k ≥ (4 + 2β)/(ε²/2 − ε³/3) · log n and the matrix entries are independent ±1, or √3 times {+1, 0, −1} with probabilities 1/6, 2/3, 1/6. This is the same k₀ as the best bound for Gaussian projections. The proof shows that every even moment of a unit vector's projection is at most that of the all-equal vector (1, …, 1)/√d, and that this vector's moments are at most the Gaussian ones. | Read |
| [NOTE-927](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-927.md) | Lee & Naor — extending Lipschitz functions via random metric partitions | A random partition of a metric space whose pieces are small and whose points are, on average, far from piece boundaries yields a "gentle" partition of unity, and averaging a Lipschitz map over it extends the map into any Banach space. This gives ae(X) ≤ C log n/log log n for every n-point metric space X (Theorem 1.10), improving Johnson, Lindenstrauss and Schechtman's C log n; ae(X) ≤ C log λ(X) for doubling X; ae ≤ C r² on K_r-minor-free graph metrics; e(ℓ₂ᵈ, Z) ≤ C√d; and, with the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, eₙ(L₂, Z) ≤ C√(log n). For maps into Hilbert space it does not improve Johnson and Lindenstrauss's K√(log n), and it leaves √(log n) open. | Read |
| [NOTE-928](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-928.md) | Linial, London & Rabinovich — the geometry of graphs | Every n-point metric embeds in ℓ₂ with distortion O(log n) in O(log n) dimensions (Theorem 3.2(1), attributed to Bourgain). The paper reproves the distortion bound by a randomized Bourgain-style construction into ℓ_p^{O(log² n)}, and it gets the dimension from Johnson–Lindenstrauss. Every embedding of a constant-degree expander into ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, of any dimension, has distortion Ω(log n) (Proposition 4.2), so the bound is tight. The lower bound comes from Leighton and Rao's flow–cut gap, and the same embeddings give an O(log k) max-flow/min-cut gap for k commodities. | Read |
| [NOTE-929](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-929.md) | Alon & Klartag — optimal compression of approximate inner products | Storing every inner product and squared distance of n points of norm at most 1 in R^k to additive error ε takes Θ(n log n/ε²) bits once k ≥ log n/ε², Θ(nk log(2 + log n/(ε²k))) for log n ≤ k ≤ log n/ε², and Θ(nk log(1/ε)) below, for 1/n^0.49 ≤ ε ≤ 0.1. Comparing these counts across dimensions shows that some n points in R^k cannot be mapped into fewer than Ω(min{k, log(2 + ε²n)/ε²}) dimensions with additive error ε, for every ε ≥ 2/√n. A bipartite version of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma reaches O(log(2 + ε²n)/ε²) dimensions; the one-family version at that size is left open. | Read |
| [NOTE-930](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-930.md) v2 | Johnson & Lindenstrauss — extensions of Lipschitz mappings into a Hilbert space | Lemma 1: any n points in ℓ₂ⁿ map into ℓ₂ᵏ, k = [K(τ) log n], with ‖f‖_lip‖f⁻¹‖_lip ≤ (1+τ)/(1−τ), by a Haar-random rank-k orthogonal projection, with positive probability. The proof concentrates the norm of a projected unit vector about its median by Lévy's isoperimetric inequality and takes a union bound over the normalized differences of the points; K ≥ (10/τ)² suffices. The lemma is a tool for Theorem 1: Lipschitz maps from n-point subsets of any metric space into ℓ₂ extend to the whole space with Lipschitz constant at most C(log n)^{1/2} times the original. | Read |
| [NOTE-931](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-931.md) | Baraniuk, Davenport, DeVore & Wakin — a simple proof of the restricted isometry property | If an n × N random matrix satisfies the concentration inequality used in JL proofs, Pr(\|‖Φx‖² − ‖x‖²\| ≥ ε‖x‖²) ≤ 2e^{−n c₀(ε)}, then a union bound over a (12/δ)^k-point net on each of the C(N, k) ≤ (eN/k)^k coordinate k-subspaces, with a short bootstrapping step from net to subspace, gives the restricted isometry property for all k ≤ c₁n/log(N/k) with probability at least 1 − 2e^{−c₂n} (Theorem 5.2). Gaussian, ±1 and Achlioptas's sparse ensembles qualify with c₀(ε) = ε²/4 − ε³/6, and the same argument gives the property in any fixed orthonormal basis. | Read |
| [NOTE-932](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-932.md) | Dasgupta & Gupta — an elementary proof of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma | For n points in ℝᵈ and 0 < ε < 1, a projection onto a random k-dimensional subspace, scaled by √(d/k), keeps every squared pairwise distance within a factor 1 ± ε with probability at least 1/n once k ≥ 4(ε²/2 − ε³/3)⁻¹ ln n. The proof bounds each tail of the squared length of a random unit vector's first k coordinates by Markov's inequality on an exponential of Gaussian squares, and then takes a union bound over the n(n−1)/2 pairs. | Read |
| [NOTE-933](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-933.md) | Donoho & Tanner — observed universality of phase transitions | For Gaussian matrices, ℓ1 minimization (and its nonnegative LP form) recovers a k-sparse vector from n random measurements in dimension N with probability tending to 1 below a curve ρ(δ; Q) in the plane δ = n/N, ρ = k/n, and to 0 above it; this was proved earlier and is restated here as Theorem 2.1. In 2,948,000 linear programs over eight non-Gaussian ensembles at N = 200, 400 and 1600, the 50% success points fall on the same curves, but exact finite-N agreement is rejected: the differences from the Gaussian decay as N^(-1/2), so the paper supports only an asymptotic ("weak") universality, as an observation, not a theorem. | Read |
| [NOTE-965](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-965.md) | Rauh, Bertschinger, Olbrich and Jost — Reconsidering unique information | Theorem 2: no redundancy function on the Williams–Beer lattice satisfies symmetry, self-redundancy, monotonicity, non-negative atoms and the identity axiom. In XORCOPY (two independent bits, their XOR, and the target their joint copy) identity forces three 1-bit atoms {i}{jk} under a 2-bit total, so {12}{13}{23} ≤ −1. Bertschinger et al.'s bivariate measures cannot be extended to that lattice. Their unique information is monotone in each argument as expected; their shared and synergistic information violate left monotonicity. | Read |
| [NOTE-969](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-969.md) | Eyink and Aluie — Localness of energy cascade I | Builds an exact band-pass decomposition of kinetic energy from smooth filters, a multiscale Germano identity, in which each band's energy changes by the flux into it minus the flux out. It then restates, with heuristic sketches, Eyink's (2005) bounds: under a scaling hypothesis on velocity increments with exponents strictly between 0 and 1, the mean energy flux across ℓ takes at most O((ℓ/Δ)^(2/3)) from scales above Δ and O((δ/ℓ)^(2/3)) from scales below δ. It argues, without proof, and checks on one 512³ simulation, that sign cancellations give Kraichnan's faster 4/3 decay. Locality here is in scale, for one field. Nothing in it bears on units. | Read |
| [NOTE-973](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-973.md) | Parish and Duraisamy — Non-Markovian closure for LES via Mori–Zwanzig | Derives large-eddy-simulation closures from the Mori–Zwanzig identity by Stinis's finite-memory approximation, which turns the memory integral into auxiliary relaxation equations, a finite Markovian augmentation of the resolved modes. Its error is not bounded and its memory length is fitted (Burgers: τ₀ ≈ 0.2 over the spectral radius of the resolved Jacobian) or preset. Against filtered DNS it matches dynamic Smagorinsky on isotropic turbulence and channel flow, beats Smagorinsky and the t-model on the Taylor–Green vortex, and puts the subgrid drain at the cutoff, as DNS does. | Read |
| [NOTE-974](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-974.md) v2 | Isett — A proof of Onsager's conjecture | The negative half of Onsager's conjecture. For every α < 1/3 there is a nonzero weak solution of the 3D incompressible Euler equations on the periodic box, in C^α in space and time, that vanishes outside a finite time interval and so does not conserve energy. It is built by iterating a Main Lemma that first glues exact local Euler solutions so that the error lives on separated short time intervals, then cancels each piece with a single transported Mikado-flow wave. For the record, it shows that a coarse-grained energy flux can survive the limit of vanishing scale for rough fields; it does not show a one-way dissipative cascade, since these solutions gain energy and then lose it. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-975](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-975.md) | Chorin, Hald and Kupferman — Optimal prediction with memory | Writes the resolved components of an ODE with random unresolved initial data as an exact generalized Langevin equation (Markovian term, memory, noise) under three projections, and approximates the memory two ways: by solving a Volterra equation for its expansion coefficients from Monte Carlo correlation functions, and by the t-damping (t-model) equation dΦ/dt = R(Φ) + tS(Φ), which needs no prior data. On one 4-variable Hamiltonian example both restore the decay of the conditional mean that the Markovian truncation misses, the Volterra scheme to about t ≈ 8. No error bound for any approximation, and no Markovian augmentation. | Read |
| [NOTE-977](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-977.md) | Shpak, Stadler, Wagner and Altenberg — Simon–Ando decomposability and fitness landscapes | States Simon and Ando's (1961) theorem for x(t+1) = (A* + εC)x, with A* block-diagonal, as existence statements: as ε → 0 the non-leading eigenvectors approach the blocks', and times T0 < T1 < T2 < T3 exist that separate within-block relaxation, quasi-equilibrium, aggregate cross-block dynamics and global equilibrium. No rate in ε and no bound on aggregation error is given. It then applies an entrywise proxy (minimal within-class rate ≫ maximal cross-class rate) to mutation–selection on hypercubes, which low mutation rates meet trivially, and to recombination, which rarely meets it. It concludes that Simon–Ando aggregation is one source of dynamical sufficiency among several, distinct from symmetry (equitable partitions) and from linkage-equilibrium character aggregation. | Read |
| [NOTE-979](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-979.md) | Shpak, Stadler, Wagner and Hermisson — Aggregation of variables and system decomposition | Separates aggregation of variables, a lower-dimensional map y = Qx whose dynamics close, from decomposition into non-interacting subsets: either can hold without the other. For a linear system the aggregate operator must satisfy ĀQ = QA. For a partition, the block sums close for every state exactly when the partition is column-equitable. Equitable partitions of mutation–selection matrices reduce single- and two-peak fitness landscapes exactly, and fail for three or more peaks unless the classes are refined to overlap classes. Simon–Ando aggregation is treated as the approximate limiting case, without error bounds. | Read |
| [NOTE-980](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-980.md) | No, Ingber and Weissman — Strong successive refinability | Extends successive refinement to second order. For finite alphabets, a two-stage code can reach both decoders' rates with their dispersion terms if the source is successively refinable throughout a neighbourhood of its law (Corollary 6), which holds for any discrete source under Hamming distortion; the Gaussian under squared error is shown directly. Layered codes then use L_n refinement stages to cut encoding complexity, at a rate penalty of order L_n log n / n, for binary and Gaussian sources. It does not treat logarithmic loss, which the reading that named it had recalled; the log-loss refinability result is No and Weissman's, concerns direct log-loss with soft reconstructions of the source itself, and does not reach the information bottleneck, whose loss is remote. | Read |
| [NOTE-982](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-982.md) | Constantin, E and Titi — Onsager's conjecture on energy conservation | A one-page proof that a weak solution of the 3D incompressible Euler equations on the periodic box conserves energy if it lies in L³(0,T; B^α_{3,∞}) ∩ C([0,T]; L²) with α > 1/3. The flux of energy into scales below a mollification scale ε is written exactly as a commutator, (u⊗u)^ε − u^ε⊗u^ε = r_ε − (u−u^ε)⊗(u−u^ε), of size ε^(2α), against a gradient of size ε^(α−1), so the flux is O(ε^(3α−1)) and vanishes. This is the positive half of Onsager's conjecture only. It does not show that rougher solutions dissipate. Two printed formulas in the manuscript are wrong as typeset, without effect on the result. | Read |
| [NOTE-984](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-984.md) | Coifman and Maggioni — Diffusion wavelets | A self-adjoint diffusion operator T with spectrum in [0, 1] defines a multiresolution analysis by thresholding its dyadic powers at a precision ε: V_j is spanned by the eigenvectors with λ^{t_j} ≥ ε, so the V_j are exactly nested spectral subspaces and the wavelet spaces W_j are spectral bands, about one octave of the generator each. The paper's contribution is an algorithm that builds localized orthonormal bases for approximations of these spaces without computing eigenvectors, by squaring the operator on each compressed basis. As written, that algorithm thresholds T^{2^{j−1}}, not T^{2^j−1} as the paper states, and the paper's own Fig. 9 follows the former. Localization, stability and the near-linear complexity are argued or observed, not proved for the compressed algorithm. | Read |
| [NOTE-985](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-985.md) | Coifman and Lafon — Diffusion maps | A symmetric non-negative kernel normalized into a reversible Markov chain gives a family of diffusion distances D_t, one per number of steps t, and an embedding by eigenvectors weighted by λ_l^t in which Euclidean distance is D_t. An α-normalization by a kernel density estimate makes the small-bandwidth limit the graph Laplacian with a density potential (α = 0), the Langevin generator whose invariant density is the sampling density (α = 1/2) or the Laplace–Beltrami operator (α = 1). The truncation is claimed accurate to relative precision δ, which is wrong: the bound is absolute. Several displays carry errors, and the heat-kernel proof has a gap. | Read |
| [NOTE-986](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-986.md) | Nadler, Lafon, Coifman and Kevrekidis — Diffusion maps and reaction coordinates | Ties diffusion maps to the dynamics that generated the data. For samples from p = e^{−U}, the small-ε generator of the α-normalized walk is Δψ − 2(1 − α)∇ψ·∇U: the graph Laplacian (α = 0) gives Fokker–Planck with potential 2U, α = 1/2 gives the Langevin dynamics with potential U itself, and α = 1 gives Laplace–Beltrami. So the slow eigenfunctions of the α = 1/2 map approximate the slow modes of the sampled stochastic system, and the paper proposes them as reaction coordinates. The expansions are formal, and with the paper's kernel every printed generator is too large by a factor of two. Its double-well example is separable. From equilibrium samples the slow eigenfunction is recovered well and the slow eigenvalue is not. That slow eigenfunctions are closed in mean, and in law only under a condition, is the record's addition. | Read |
| [NOTE-989](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-989.md) | Chorin, Hald and Kupferman — Optimal prediction and the Mori–Zwanzig representation | Writes Zwanzig's nonlinear Mori–Zwanzig identity with the projection taken as conditional expectation on the resolved variables under an invariant measure: ∂ₜSᵗA = R(SᵗA) + ∫₀ᵗ K(s, S^{t−s}A) ds + S⊥ᵗF, with R(A) = E[LA\|A], F = LA − E[LA\|A] and K(s, A) = E[LS⊥ˢF\|A]. First-order optimal prediction, dv/dt = R(v), is that identity with the memory and noise dropped, and for a canonical Hamiltonian system it is Hamiltonian in a renormalized 𝓗 = −log∫e^{−H}. In a perturbative nonlinear Schrödinger example with one resolved mode, a memory kernel cut off at a hand-chosen time recovers the decay of the conditional mean that the Markovian scheme misses. The paper states no fluctuation–dissipation relation and no criterion for when the Markovian term suffices. | Read |
| [NOTE-1010](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1010.md) | Random Hyperbolic Graphs: Degree Sequence and Clustering | Proves for the threshold hyperbolic random graph (curvature −1, density exponent α > 1/2, R = 2 log n + C) that the average local clustering coefficient is Θ(1) with high probability and that the degree sequence is a power law with exponent 2α + 1 up to the maximum degree n^(1/(2α)+o(1)), with exact asymptotics for the fraction of each degree. Skimmed: the statements and the method were read, the proofs only in outline. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1011](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1011.md) | Clustering and the hyperbolic geometry of complex networks | For Krioukov et al.'s hyperbolic random graph with 0 < ζ/α < 2, proves that below temperature 1 (β > 1) the global clustering coefficient converges to an explicit positive constant when ζ/α < 1 and to zero when 1 ≤ ζ/α < 2, and that at or above temperature 1 it converges to zero; clustering among vertices of bounded type stays positive for all ζ/α < 2 when β > 1. Skimmed: §1 and the theorem statements read, the proofs not. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1013](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1013.md) v2 | Buckmaster, De Lellis, Székelyhidi and Vicol — Onsager's conjecture for admissible weak solutions | The admissible version of the negative half of Onsager's conjecture. For every β < 1/3 and every smooth strictly positive e(t) on [0, T] there is a C^β weak solution of 3D Euler on the torus with ∫\|v\|² = e(t) exactly, so with e decreasing the energy only falls and the coarse-grained flux runs into vanishing scales on every time interval ([THEORY-776](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-776.md)). That is the one-way transfer Isett's solutions lacked, but one-way only for the box as a whole (no local energy inequality), and chosen by the prescribed profile, since an increasing e works just as well. | Read |
| [NOTE-1020](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1020.md) | Del Vecchio and Slotine — Contraction and singular perturbation | Contraction gives global, explicit, uniform-in-time bounds for singular perturbation: the fast state reaches an εχ_z(d + K)/λ_z neighbourhood of the slow manifold at rate λ_z/ε, and the reduced (quasi-steady-state) trajectory is O(ε)-accurate for all time. Theorem 3 as printed is false: it needs the reduced system, not f alone, to be contracting. The robustness lemma is proved for constant metrics only; the reading re-derives it for state- and time-dependent ones, and with it the two steps [THEORY-771](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-771.md) lacked. | Read |
| [NOTE-1022](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1022.md) | Giri, Kwon and Novack — The L³-based strong Onsager theorem | The L³-based strong Onsager theorem: for every β < 1/3 there are weak Euler solutions in C⁰_t(B^β_{3,∞} ∩ L^{1/(1−3β)}) satisfying the local energy inequality and strictly dissipating total energy. In the proof the Duchon–Robert measure is exactly the smooth density −e e′ρ₀², positive in a periodic array of pipes and zero outside, fixed at the first step; so the coarse-grained flux into vanishing scales is one-signed locally in space and time, in the limit ([THEORY-772](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-772.md)), with its place and rate chosen by the construction. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1025](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1025.md) | Bousquet and Slotine — Contraction and near-decomposability | Under contraction of the fast modules and of the reduced slow system, and coupling terms bounded affinely in the off-manifold state, a nearly decomposable system stays within O(ε) of its singular-perturbation reduction, uniformly in time after a transient of order (1/β_f + 1/(εβ_g)) log(1/ε), for ε below an explicit critical separation ε_c. Deterministic trajectory error only. Remark 8 prints ε_c inverted, and the slow-error bound needs an unstated d_g = 0. | Read |
| [NOTE-1027](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1027.md) | Isett — Continuous, globally dissipative Euler flows | The first continuous weak Euler solutions satisfying the local energy inequality with nonzero dissipation: C^α_{t,x}, α < 1/15, on T^d, d ≥ 3, with a Cantor family sharing one initial datum and one dissipation measure. In the construction that measure is a function of time alone, so the coarse-grained flux into vanishing scales is one-way at every place in the limit and uniform in space, switched on only while the solution is drained to zero ([THEORY-821](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-821.md)). | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1028](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1028.md) | Chorin and Lu — Discrete stochastic parametrization by NARMAX | Model reduction done wholly in discrete time: advance the resolved variables by a fixed integrator and fit the exact one-step discrepancy as a NARMAX series, so memory lives in a few lags of the discrepancy, the resolved variable and the innovations. On Lorenz 96 with ε = 0.5 one or two lags reproduce x₁'s statistics and double forecast lead time at δ = 0.05. The link to Mori–Zwanzig is analogy, not derivation; nothing is proved and no error is bounded. The record's check: a partially observed linear Gaussian VAR(1) is exactly ARMA, with order 1 + the rank of its MZ memory kernels, so a memory non-zero at every lag is carried exactly by finitely many history-measurable coordinates. | Read |
| [NOTE-1029](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1029.md) | Lin and Lu — Wiener projections and the Koopman–Mori–Zwanzig formalism | An exact link between Mori–Zwanzig and NARMAX, with the approximation named. For an invertible map with an invariant measure, projecting onto the whole past of chosen functions of the resolved variables removes the memory term: the reduced equation is the causal Wiener filter on the coarse variable's own history, with a residual orthogonal to all of it. NARMAX follows only by an "uncontrolled" rational approximation of the filter; no error is bounded. The record's checks: Mori's kernels and the Wiener filter are both fixed by the coarse variable's autocovariance; for a scalar coarse variable of a linear Gaussian VAR(1) both are rational with the same numerator, the rational form is exact, and the memory Hankel rank is d − 1 for any rational autocovariance of rank d. | Read |
| [NOTE-1030](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1030.md) | Rosas et al. — Software in the natural world | Three exact closures of a coarse-graining Z of a stationary discrete process X, built from computational mechanics. Informational closure (the micro past adds nothing to predicting Z, which is Barnett–Seth dynamical independence) is proved equivalent to causal closure (Z's ε-machine equals its υ-machine). For spatial maps it implies computational closure (Z's ε-machine is a coarse-graining of X's), and the converse fails. For Markov chains closure is tied to strong lumpability. The proofs of the main equivalences hold, re-derived in [THEORY-820](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-820.md) and [THEORY-822](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-822.md). The lattice claims are asserted and in part false. Several examples contain slips. The modular random walk closes by symmetry, not modularity. Nothing is said about approximate closure. | Read |
| [NOTE-1059](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1059.md) | Lee-Youngzie et al. — Towards a mathematical structure of global phenomenal consciousness | A hypothesis article with no data. It maps the parts of an experience, ordered by subsumption into a finite topology, to similarity-judgement matrices of their qualia by a presheaf, and reads compatibility of narrow qualia on overlaps as the condition for phenomenal binding, and the presheaf's being a sheaf as the broad quale's being determined by its parts. It reads a sheaf failure as disunity in binocular rivalry and as context dependence in the Ebbinghaus illusion, and gives no rule for telling the two apart. Its worked topology example is malformed, and by its own definitions disagreement on an overlap is not a sheaf failure. | Read |
| [NOTE-1099](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1099.md) | Statistical ranking and combinatorial Hodge theory | Rank aggregation as combinatorial Hodge theory. Aggregated pairwise comparisons form an edge flow, and its orthogonal decomposition gives a least-squares global ranking (the gradient), local inconsistency (curl) and global inconsistency (harmonic). The size of the cyclic residual certifies whether any global ranking is meaningful. The framework is cardinal, generalizes Borda, and is not Kemeny. | Read |
| [NOTE-1112](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1112.md) | Theory of Value: An Axiomatic Analysis of Economic Equilibrium | Read for §4.6 only. Not every complete preorder has a utility function: the lexicographic ordering of R² has none. Under a continuity assumption (closed upper and lower contour sets), a complete preorder on a connected subset of Rˡ, and more generally on a connected separable space, has a continuous utility function, and conversely. Debreu credits the separable form to Eilenberg (1941), and his own 1954 paper for dropping connectedness on second-countable spaces. Utility is defined only up to increasing transformation. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1116](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1116.md) | Flows and Decompositions of Games: Harmonic and Potential Games | A finite game is read as a flow, the unilateral payoff differences on the graph of strategy profiles, and the Helmholtz decomposition of that flow splits the game uniquely into potential, harmonic and nonstrategic parts. Potential games are those with no harmonic part. Harmonic games, the pure-conflict part, generically have no pure equilibrium. The nearest potential game is a closed-form l2 projection. | Read |
| [NOTE-1155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1155.md) | Balduzzi et al. — Re-evaluating evaluation | A methods paper with two short applications. It reads evaluation data as antisymmetric matrices. Elo is then the row mean of the log-odds, exact when they are curl-free and movable by copies, and the Schur decomposition gives a multidimensional Elo. Nash averaging scores agents and tasks against the maximum-entropy Nash equilibrium of a zero-sum meta-game. Its proved invariance covers exact copies, and only when that equilibrium is unique. A checked counterexample shows what happens otherwise. | Read |
| [NOTE-1215](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1215.md) | Ashwin, Wieczorek, Vitolo & Cox — Tipping points in open systems | A classification and a criterion, not an empirical study. Tipping in an open system ẋ = f(x, λ(t)) is split into B-tipping (a bifurcation of the quasi-static attractor), N-tipping (noise carries the system out of its neighbourhood) and R-tipping, where "the system fails to track a continuously changing quasi-static attractor". In a linear model with a fixed stable M and a tipping radius R, the attractor never changes stability, yet steady drift r tips the system when ‖M‖⁻¹\|r\| > R and cannot when ‖M⁻¹‖\|r\| < R. Three examples, one with a unique globally stable equilibrium, and a global energy balance model show each type alone. Neither N- nor R-tipping needs any change of stability, so there is no reason to expect critical-slowing warnings for them. | Read |
| [NOTE-1217](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1217.md) | Stewart, Golubitsky & Pivato — Symmetry groupoids and patterns of synchrony | In a coupled cell network, an equivalence relation on the cells gives a synchrony subspace invariant under every vector field the network admits if and only if it is balanced: every two equivalent cells have an input isomorphism that maps each input to an equivalent one (Theorem 6.5). Symmetry is one source of balance, not the only one, so robust synchrony occurs in networks with no symmetry. The dynamics on such a subspace are admissible for a smaller quotient network (Theorem 9.2), which can have a symmetry the original lacks. The paper treats existence only, not stability, and says so. | Read |
| [NOTE-1218](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1218.md) | Torres-Hugas et al. — Cycle holonomy and remote synchronization | For a phase model whose edges carry antisymmetric phase lags, the twisted Laplacian Lα = δα*δα has a zero mode exactly when every cycle holonomy is 0 mod 2π, and otherwise its smallest eigenvalue measures the residual incompatibility; for an isolated ℓ-cycle that eigenvalue is largest at holonomy π. The symmetric Sakaguchi–Kuramoto model is a different model, but on cactus graphs its lag gives each ℓ-cycle a path mismatch (ℓ − 2)α, which an associated connection is built to carry as holonomy. In the triangle–pentagon remote-synchronization motif, the pentagon's mismatch reaches π at α = π/3, where the locked branch is exactly a two-group state; but the branch has already lost transverse stability at αc ≈ 1.0164, so the holonomy marks geometry, not stability. | Read |
| [NOTE-1221](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1221.md) | Robinson — Sheaves are the canonical data structure for sensor integration | An expository paper. It posits six axioms for an integrated sensor system and defines a sheaf as whatever satisfies them, so "canonical" is argued by that axiomatization, not proved; the paper itself calls sheaves one of "many co-universal information representations". Its tools need less than a sheaf: on a presheaf of pseudometric spaces, the consistency radius of an assignment (the largest disagreement between an observation and the restriction of another) bounds its distance to every global section below by ε/(1 + K) when the restrictions are K-Lipschitz, and data fusion is the search for the nearest global section. In one simulated search-and-rescue scenario fusion cut the crash-location error 2–8×, and the per-restriction discrepancies singled out a biased sensor by inspection. Cohomology, for linear sheaves, flags configurations that can be locally but not globally consistent. | Read |
| [NOTE-1222](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1222.md) | Hansen & Ghrist — Opinion dynamics on discourse sheaves | A discourse sheaf gives each agent a private opinion space and each edge a discourse space, with a linear expression map from each agent into each of its edges. Opinion diffusion by the sheaf Laplacian converges to the projection onto the global sections: agreement in what neighbours express, not in what they hold. Letting the expression maps diffuse instead converges to the nearest sheaf in which the fixed opinions agree in expression, which the authors call "learning to lie". Nothing in the dynamics checks expression against what is held, so the agreement reached is coherence, not accuracy. | Read |
| [NOTE-1223](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1223.md) | Baez & Fong — A compositional framework for passive linear networks | Open passive linear circuits (resistors, inductors and capacitors, the latter two through the Laplace transform over the field R(s)) are the morphisms of a hypergraph category Circ of decorated cospans, and black-boxing, which keeps only the Lagrangian relation a circuit imposes between its terminals' potentials and currents, is a hypergraph functor Circ → LagRel (Thm 1.1, Thm 7.7). The relation is the graph of the differential of the power functional, the Dirichlet form left when the interior nodes are eliminated by the principle of minimum power; series resistors are the worked example. Dirichlet forms alone compose by that elimination but have no identities, so the target is Lagrangian relations. | Read |
| [NOTE-1224](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1224.md) | Singer — Angular synchronization | Angles θ₁, …, θₙ are estimated, up to one global phase, from noisy offsets θᵢ − θⱼ of which an unknown fraction are pure outliers, by the top eigenvector of the Hermitian matrix Hᵢⱼ = e^{iδᵢⱼ} or by an SDP like Goemans–Williamson's. On the complete graph a random-matrix argument puts the eigenvector's threshold at p > 1/√n good offsets, with the expected squared correlation near 1/(1 + 1/(np²)). Fano's inequality shows no algorithm can do much better: the information bound is of order √(n/m), and the polynomial method's threshold is within a factor √((L − 1)/(2 log₂ L)) of it, where 2π/L is the angular resolution, while exhaustive maximum likelihood costs O(mLⁿ). | Read |
| [NOTE-1225](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1225.md) | Spivak — Compositional dynamics in learning and mechanics | A category-theoretic syntax, the operad ArrSm of "smooth adaptive arrangements" (a responsive parameter space, a lens of output and input maps between manifolds, and a real potential), with two functorial semantics into polynomial coalgebras, i.e. discrete-time input-output machines. They differ only in the integrator: Φconf stores position and takes a descent step, Φphase stores position and momentum and takes a symplectic-Euler step. Φconf turns a parameterized map plus a loss into gradient descent with backpropagation, and a closed system with inverse-Hessian response into Newton's method. One arrangement of harmonic particles on a finite directed graph gives the discrete wave equation under Φphase and the discrete heat equation under Φconf, both governed by the symmetrized graph Laplacian. The main technical result is lens internalization, a lax symmetric monoidal functor Lens_C → C. | Read |
| [NOTE-1231](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1231.md) | Clarke, Grumberg, Jha, Lu & Veith — Counterexample-guided abstraction refinement | A model checker runs on an existential abstraction that merges concrete states, so a property true of the abstraction is true of the program (Theorem 1). An abstract counterexample is checked against the concrete system by image computation; if it has no concrete counterpart, the first abstract state where it breaks is split to separate the concrete states reachable along it from those with the transition onward, and checking runs again. The coarsest such split is stated to be NP-hard (proof omitted), so a polynomial, non-optimal split is used. For finite-state programs and ACTL* properties whose counterexamples are paths or loops, the loop ends in a real counterexample or a proof. The property is fixed throughout. | Read |
| [NOTE-1233](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1233.md) | Hansen & Ghrist — Toward a spectral theory of cellular sheaves | An exploratory programme, not a single result: the Hodge Laplacian of a weighted cellular sheaf, whose kernel in degree k is the cohomology H^k (in degree 0, the global sections), with sheaf versions of spectral graph theory's basics: harmonic extension, an eigenvalue bound for normalized sheaves, interlacing, pushforward and covering spectra, product spectra, effective resistance and a sparsification theorem. The heat flow ẋ = −Δ^k x converges exponentially to the orthogonal projection onto the harmonic cochains (Prop. 8.1). Kron reduction fails for general sheaves, because an interior vertex can impose constraints on the boundary that no pairwise sheaf expresses. A Cheeger inequality is not proved; the applications in §8 are sketches. | Read |
| [NOTE-1323](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1323.md) | Alvarez-Melis et al. — Hyperbolic OT hierarchy matching | Two Poincaré embeddings of the same WordNet hierarchy, from different random seeds, differ by more than a hyperbolic isometry: branches move relative to one another and pairwise distances change. Euclidean aligners and hyperbolic OT with an orthogonal map therefore fail (P@10 at most 11% across languages). Registering one space with a hyperbolic neural network trained through a Sinkhorn divergence recovers P@10 of 38–60% across languages and P@1 of 22% when matching a hierarchy to itself. The matching uses the symmetric hyperbolic distance, and nothing in it preserves the direction of entailment. | Read |
| [NOTE-1324](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1324.md) | Alvarez-Melis et al. — Structured optimal transport | Replaces the linear cost of discrete optimal transport by the Lovász extension of a submodular set function on assignments, so that the cost of a coupling depends on which assignments are made together. The problem stays convex and is a zero-sum game against cost matrices in the base polytope, solved by saddle-point mirror prox with Sinkhorn and base-polytope projections; it reduces to ordinary OT when the set function is modular. Its own example cost, eq. (12), is not concave, so the cost it defines is not submodular. | Read |
| [NOTE-1325](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1325.md) | Flamary et al. — POT | A software paper for POT, an MIT-licensed Python library of optimal transport solvers: exact transport by a C++ solver, entropic transport by Sinkhorn and stabilized variants, Wasserstein barycenters, partial and unbalanced transport, regularized transport, Gromov–Wasserstein, sliced Wasserstein and domain adaptation, with tests covering 92% of lines. It reports no experiments. Fused and partial Gromov–Wasserstein and co-optimal transport, which the record uses POT for, are not in this paper; they came in later releases. | Read |
| [NOTE-1326](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1326.md) | Sarkar, Mukherjee and Sato — Relational composition as parallel transport | The companion paper's premise, stated by its authors: per-entity frame freedom is "a chosen inductive bias, not a consequence of fresh names". Under it, scores go through ⟨xᵢ, Tᵢⱼxⱼ⟩ and transports must be supplied. Its parsed-benchmark controls show the premise's orthogonality helping on StepGame and costing 64.6 points on CLUTRR. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1327](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1327.md) | Yu et al. — AvAtar active OT alignment | For alignment by entropic optimal transport, AvAtar picks which source objects to send to an oracle, who names each one's true match. It scores a candidate by the derivative of a proxy utility of the transport plan (how near a permutation, or how consistent with the graphs, the plan is) with respect to supervising each possible match, averaged over matches by the current plan. The derivative is exact, from one singular positive semidefinite linear system solved by conjugate gradients. At a fixed budget of 20% extra labels on top of 20% given, it beats uncertainty baselines by up to 2.8 MRR points and random choice by up to 16, without variances reported. | Read |
| [NOTE-1328](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1328.md) | Vayer et al. — Fused Gromov–Wasserstein | FGW compares two attributed graphs with one coupling whose cost mixes, with weight α, a Wasserstein term on node features and a Gromov–Wasserstein term on structure. For α in (0, 1), q = 1 and distance-matrix structures it is a metric that vanishes exactly when a bijection preserves weights, features and structure. As α tends to 0 or 1 it tends to W or GW. On benchmark graph classification it is competitive with graph kernels, but the supplement shows Wasserstein on features alone matching or beating it on several datasets. | Read |
| [NOTE-1329](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1329.md) | Hashimoto et al. — Word embeddings as metric recovery | If text were generated by a random walk whose steps depend on distance in a latent Euclidean or Riemannian space, negative log co-occurrence over a window that grows with the vocabulary, less a term for each word, would approach the squared latent distance. GloVe, word2vec and the PMI-SVD method then have the true embedding among their optima, up to isometry and unigram terms, and a negative-binomial regression on the same relation embeds words and manifolds about as well. On real corpora the evidence for a Euclidean semantic space is a correlation of 0.75 between PMI and human similarity ratings and two nearest-neighbour statistics; the authors say the random walk is not a model of language. | Read |
| [NOTE-1330](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1330.md) | Chowdhury & Mémoli — Network Gromov–Wasserstein | The Gromov–Wasserstein distance, defined by minimizing the distortion of a coupling, is a pseudometric on all measure networks: any Polish node set with a probability measure and any bounded, possibly asymmetric, edge-weight function. It is zero exactly when the two networks are weakly isomorphic, that is, when both are images of one network that preserves weights and measures. Cheap invariants give a hierarchy of lower bounds, and the third lower bound, a transport problem whose costs are themselves transport problems, reduces to one-dimensional transport in closed form. The bounds are one-sided: networks can agree on every invariant and still be apart. | Read |
| [NOTE-1331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1331.md) | Sarkar, Mukherjee and Sato — Attention as lattice gauge theory | Under per-entity O(d) frame freedom, transports carry invariant information only around cycles, a triangle's invariants are class functions of its holonomy, and an equivariant edge update is Ψ(H)Tᵢⱼ with Ψ conjugation-equivariant: a sound conditional theorem, standard in lattice gauge theory and synchronization, whose "unique form" is a family. The untrained S4 experiments show composition doing the work and Wilson-loop routing adding 0.6–7.8 points; the 0.99 AUC is a ceiling the data's construction sets, as the paper itself computes. | Read |
| [NOTE-1332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1332.md) | Bodnar et al. — Neural sheaf diffusion | Bodnar et al. read sheaf diffusion on a graph as a projection onto the harmonic space of a sheaf Laplacian and ask which classes of restriction maps can make that projection linearly separate a node labelling. A symmetric one-dimensional sheaf, which is a weighted graph Laplacian, cannot separate the two sides of a balanced bipartite graph; signed maps separate any two classes; no one-dimensional sheaf separates three; diagonal maps with d ≥ C stalks, and O(d) bundles for C ≤ 2d at d = 2 and 4, separate any number. Every one of these sheaves is built from the labels. Learned from features, such sheaves give competitive node classification on six small heterophilic benchmarks. The claim that the O(d) construction exists only at d = 2 and 4 is wrong: it works at d = 8 too. | Read |
| [NOTE-1333](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1333.md) | Alvarez-Melis et al. — OT with global invariances | Optimal transport between two unregistered spaces is posed as a joint minimisation over couplings and one global linear map from a Schatten ℓp ball. Under angle preservation or whitening it reduces to maximising a dual Schatten norm of the transported cross-covariance XΓYᵀ: the nuclear norm for orthogonal maps (p = ∞) and the Frobenius norm for p = 2, which is exactly GW with cosine similarity and squared loss. Alternating SVD and Sinkhorn steps with annealed entropy solve it without adversarial initialisation. On word translation it is level with GW and behind self-learning on nine of ten directions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1334](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1334.md) v2 | Zeng et al. — HOT multi-network alignment | Aligns K networks at once by one multi-marginal coupling tensor. The networks are first co-clustered through a fused Gromov–Wasserstein barycenter, then each cluster's nodes are aligned by multi-marginal fused GW with a cost from anchor-based random-walk embeddings, solved by a KL proximal point method. The joint objective at any tensor is the sum of the pairwise objectives at its marginals, so it bounds the sum of pairwise optima from above. On three-network benchmarks whose true correspondences are consistent by construction, it beats pairwise and multi-network baselines in pairwise and high-order hits; no experiment isolates the joint coupling from the new cost and the clustering. | Read |
| [NOTE-1335](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1335.md) | Redko et al. — CO-Optimal Transport | COOT matches two data matrices of different shapes by optimizing two couplings at once, one between rows (samples) and one between columns (features), under a bilinear cost. With equal sizes and uniform weights it is zero exactly when the matrices are equal up to a permutation of rows and a separate permutation of columns, so its plans are determined at best up to the matrix's joint row–column symmetries; the paper proves no uniqueness. For symmetric matrices it is a lower bound on GW, equal to it for squared Euclidean distance matrices. | Read |
| [NOTE-1336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1336.md) | Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola — Gromov-Wasserstein word alignment | Unsupervised word translation is cast as a Gromov–Wasserstein problem between the two languages' intra-language cosine-similarity matrices, solved by entropic projected gradient (each step a Sinkhorn problem), with no anchors. It matches adversarial-plus-refinement methods on related languages trained on comparable corpora at a fraction of the cost, and does markedly worse on English–Russian and English–Finnish. The objective sees only within-space similarities, so it cannot distinguish a correspondence from one composed with a symmetry of either space; the paper does not say so. | Read |
| [NOTE-1342](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1342.md) | Felekis et al. — Causal optimal transport of abstractions | COTA learns a stochastic map from a low-level to a high-level causal model's state space from samples of paired interventional distributions, given both DAGs and the map between interventions, by solving one entropic optimal-transport problem per intervention with a cost that rewards compatibility with the paired interventions and a term meant to impose do-calculus relations between plans. As written, that term depends only on the plans' marginals, which the transport constraints fix, so it is constant on the feasible set and its weight acts only by rescaling the other terms. The reported gains come from the compatibility cost when interventions are many; with few, a Hamming cost does better. | Read |
| [NOTE-1343](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1343.md) | Peyré et al. — Gromov–Wasserstein averaging | Defines an entropic Gromov–Wasserstein discrepancy between similarity matrices of any size and loss, and their barycenter as a Fréchet mean of user-chosen size and weights. It is computed by alternating Sinkhorn- based coupling updates with a closed-form matrix update that, for square loss, averages the couplings' realignments of the inputs with the barycenter weights. The algorithm is proved to keep PSD and infinitely divisible kernels in their classes; its convergence at the step size used is observed, not proved, and only stationary points are sought. | Read |
| [NOTE-1348](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1348.md) | Goguen & Burstall — Institutions | An institution is a category of signatures with a sentence functor, a contravariant model functor and a satisfaction relation per signature, subject to one axiom, the Satisfaction Condition: a translated sentence holds in a model exactly when the original holds in the model's reduct. From that axiom alone theories and model classes form a Galois connection, theories can be glued by colimits whenever signatures can (Theorem 11), constraints that force standard or free interpretations can be added as sentences without losing this, and an institution morphism with surjective model translation lets a prover for one logic decide entailment for another (Proposition 35). The Satisfaction Condition is a criterion of correct translation relative to a given model translation; it says nothing about where that model translation comes from. | Read |
| [NOTE-1350](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1350.md) | Sengupta, Tozzi, Cooray, Douglas and Friston — Towards a neuronal gauge theory | An essay proposing that variational free-energy minimization be cast as a gauge theory. The only connection it names is the Levi-Civita connection of the Fisher information metric on the manifold of a belief's sufficient statistics, so its gauge freedom is reparameterization of the variational family; its claimed payoff is that attention is precision weighting forced by that manifold's curvature. No gauge group, invariant Lagrangian or compensating field is written down. | Read |
| [NOTE-1379](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1379.md) | Hofbauer and Schreiber — Permanence via invasion graphs | For ecological ODEs whose invasion growth rates have well-defined, nonzero signs on each subcommunity, it defines the invasion graph (edges S → T when every species in T but not S can invade S and every species lost cannot invade T) and proves that when the graph is acyclic, robust permanence holds if, and essentially only if, each species i has a positive invasion growth rate at every −i community. With cycles, signs are not enough. | Read |
| [NOTE-1395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1395.md) | Mehta, Cui, Wang and Marsland — Constrained optimization as ecological dynamics | Any minimization of f(R) over R ≥ 0 under constraints g_i(R) ≤ 0 has the KKT points of a consumer–resource dynamics as its steady states: variables are resources, each constraint is a species whose abundance is its Lagrange multiplier, and binding constraints are the surviving species. For quadratic programs the dynamics is MacArthur's model, and the Lagrangian dual is a generalized Lotka–Volterra system. A cavity solution then gives the statistics of random quadratic programs, in agreement with numerics at M = 100. | Read |
| [NOTE-1401](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1401.md) | Désidéri — Multiple-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) | Defines Pareto-stationarity (some convex combination of the criteria's gradients is zero), proves it necessary for Pareto-optimality, and shows that when it fails the minimum-norm element ω of the gradients' convex hull gives a direction −ω along which every criterion decreases, with (u, ω) ≥ ‖ω‖² for every u in the hull. Steepest descent along −ω, the MGDA, has a subsequence converging to a Pareto-stationary point when the criteria are positive and coercive. The direction depends on how the gradients are scaled; the author calls the right scaling open. | Read |
| [NOTE-1422](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1422.md) | Serván and Allesina — Tractable models of ecological assembly | For competitive Lotka–Volterra communities with A = D(v)BD(w), B symmetric with positive entries, assembled by rare, low-density, well-separated invasions, MacArthur's Lyapunov function V orders the feasible sub-communities, so the assembly graph is acyclic and every feasible sub-community can be assembled without extinctions; with the paper's Theorem 1 this makes sequential and all-at-once assembly reach the same end-points. One end-point when B is positive definite, several when it is not. | Read |
| [NOTE-1427](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1427.md) | Apt — Potential Games (slides) | Apt's slides define exact, ordinal and generalized ordinal potentials and the finite improvement property, and state, crediting Monderer and Shapley 1996, that a finite game has a generalized ordinal potential if and only if it has the FIP; one direction is proved and the converse sketched by counting improvement sequences. A two-by-two game with the FIP and no ordinal potential shows the equivalence cannot be with ordinal potentials. | Read |
| [NOTE-1441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1441.md) | Coifman et al. — Diffusion maps (full reading) | With the equations visible, the paper's diffusion distance is the distance induced by the symmetric kernel ã^(m), D_m² = ã^(m)(x, x) + ã^(m)(y, y) − 2ã^(m)(x, y), with ã's eigenvalues written λ_i², so that the map x ↦ (λ_i^m φ_i(x)) is an exact isometry for it. The truncation is claimed with a relative error 1 + O(e^{−αm}). Theorem 2.1, the ε → 0 heat-kernel limit of the α = 1 normalization, and the α-family (Eq. 14) are stated without proof; the sampling condition is that each ball of radius √ε hold enough points. Eq. 5 and Eq. 14 give the α = 0 potential opposite signs. | Read |
| [NOTE-1465](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1465.md) | Santolin et al. — Freidlin-Wentzell and stochastic thermodynamics | For overdamped diffusions with weak noise and a nonconservative force, the Freidlin–Wentzell quasi-potential is expanded about the detailed-balance free energy, each order integrated along the detailed-balanced relaxation, and the first order saturates the emergent second law. The weak-noise escape rate from an attractor is bracketed below by minus the entropy produced in relaxing into it and above by the entropy produced along the most likely escape path. The bracket closes at detailed balance and widens with the nonconservative force; in a sheared double well it stays usefully narrow for weak shear. | Read |
| [NOTE-1466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1466.md) | Saligrama — information before commitment in safe adaptive control | A safe adaptive controller must stay safe under every model it has not ruled out. Its first action that leaves no safe continuation under an alternative is a commitment, and the evidence for it must be in hand before the action: what that action reveals comes too late. With the information gathered before commitment measured as a KL divergence between stopped records, a data-processing argument bounds any uniformly safe policy's regret below by the cost of not committing with probability ½e^{−I_pre} − α. So bounded pre-commitment information leaves a fixed fraction of the oracle gap, and a linear gap gives linear regret. Safe recovery at O(√(T log T)) is proved when a safe experiment is repeatable, informative and returns to a common state. | Read |
| [NOTE-1476](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1476.md) | Dal Cengio, Lecomte & Polettini — Geometry of nonequilibrium reaction networks | Extends the Hill–Schnakenberg cycle analysis from linear networks (graphs) to interacting ones (hypergraphs) by row reduction of the stoichiometric matrix: cycles span its kernel and carry steady currents and non-conservative affinities, cocycles span the orthogonal complement and carry transient currents and conservative forces, with an integrator that recovers chemical potentials. One chemostat cannot drive a network; two can. Suppressing the reactions of a cocycle creates a new conserved quantity. Near equilibrium the relaxation and driven-response Onsager matrices share their spectrum, and the cycle decomposition gives a linear-regime reconstruction of metabolic fluxes that respects Kirchhoff's laws. | Read |
| [NOTE-1477](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1477.md) | Kolathaya & Ames — input-to-state safe control barrier functions | Defines input-to-state safety of a set C = {h ≥ 0}: under a bounded input disturbance d, the larger set C_d = {h + γ(‖d‖∞) ≥ 0} is forward invariant, for a class-K γ. A barrier condition with a disturbance term, ḣ ≥ −α(h) − ι(‖d‖), implies it (Theorem 1). Given an ordinary control barrier function, adding L_g hᵀ to a safeguarding controller, or the constraint term −εL_g h L_g hᵀ in a CLF–CBF quadratic program, yields such a function with ι(‖d‖) = ‖d‖²/(4ε) (Theorem 2). The enlargement is a class-K function of the disturbance bound in barrier units, quadratic in the universal construction; it is not proportional to the bound. | Read |
